text: First workday after the holidays. The Boss cheerfully: “Rested? Great, January’s plan was due yesterday.”
left: Ask for a day to warm up

text: A colleague whispers: “I forgot my computer password. And email. And, I think, my own name.”
Accounting wants December expense reports. The receipts are somewhere among the tangerines.
Three boxes of leftover party chocolates in the kitchen. The office manager asks if she should toss them.
right: Toss them — new year, new me

text: HR launches a “New year — new goals” challenge: a 30-item survey about your dreams.
The alarm rings at 7:00, but your body is sure it’s January 1st, 3 a.m.
The department discusses who gained how much over the holidays. Eyes slowly turn to you.
right: Change the topic to the report

text: The Boss wants a “strategy for the year” by tonight. All you can think of is potato salad.
The client is back from vacation and sent 47 emails in a row marked “urgent, from last year”.
right: Call and sort it all at once

text: On the call it turns out everyone’s still in pajamas — except you. You’re the only one in a shirt.
left: Admit you’re in pajama pants too

text: The department is collecting for gifts for Valentine’s Day and Defender of the Fatherland Day (Russia’s “men’s day,” Feb 23). Everyone chips in — except whoever’s counting.
An anonymous valentine on your desk: “Thanks for always submitting reports on time.” The handwriting looks suspiciously like the Boss’s.
HR runs a “Best Gift for a Colleague” contest. Budget: $5. Expectations: $50.
Minus 28 outside. The car won’t start, the bus never came, and stand-up is in 40 minutes.
right: Walk it like a polar explorer

text: A colleague gives you a shaving kit for February 23rd. Or for the 14th. He’s not sure himself.
The Boss asks you to stay late and decorate the office with hearts: “Corporate culture matters.”
February is short, but the targets are March-sized. Accounting asks how you plan to make it.
The heating is off in the office. The office manager hands out blankets — two fewer than there are people.
Coworkers invite you to a café after work to celebrate. Tomorrow at 9:00 you have a presentation.
A client wishes you a happy holiday… and asks for a discount “in honor of the holiday.”
First sunshine outside the window. You absolutely don’t want to work — you want to be outdoors.
International Women’s Day (March 8, a big deal here) is around the corner. The department argues: flowers, chocolates, or “let’s just do gift cards.”
HR announces a “spring refresh”: everyone moves to a different desk to “refresh team interaction.”
The Boss is back from a conference, inspired: “We’re launching five new projects. By April.”
right: Get fired up about all five

text: A giant icicle hangs over the office entrance. The office manager asks for “someone brave” to call building management.
A colleague has fallen in love and spends all day writing poems instead of the report. It’s a shared report.
right: Gently bring him back to earth

text: Pollen season begins. You sneeze so hard that everyone on the call gets muted.
The quarter is ending, and accounting reminds you: all invoices are due by the 25th. Today is the 24th.
Your desk neighbor has started a spring diet and crunches carrots loudly all day.
The Boss suggests holding stand-up outdoors — “it’s spring!” Wind, laptops, and 40°F.
right: Suggest a room with a window

text: Quarterly report: the Boss wants it “pretty, with charts, and showing growth.” There is no growth.
April 1st. A colleague announces the office is moving to another city. Sounds like a joke, but HR is silent.
The report numbers are off by 3 cents. The analyst says: “It’s a matter of principle.”
HR sends out a satisfaction survey. Anonymous. With your name in the link.
The client wants the quarterly summary “on one slide.” There’s data for forty.
The Boss scheduled the quarter review for Friday, 5:30 p.m. “It’ll be quick, fifteen minutes.”
The office manager invites everyone to a community clean-up around the business park. On Saturday.
The department argues over who’s to blame for missing the target. Everyone carefully glances at the intern.
Accounting found an error in your January report. It needs a backdated fix by this evening.
The intern asks what KPI means and why everyone flinches at the word.
Half the department took vacation between the May holidays. The other half is pretending to work.
A colleague is handing out tomato seedlings. Refusing is taken as a personal insult.
The Boss calls on your day off: “You’re just at the cottage anyway, check your email on your phone.”
Everyone’s heading out of town for the weekend — traffic backed up all the way to the office. You’ve been in it for an hour.
left: Join the call from the car
right: Put on music and accept it

text: HR is organizing a company picnic. They need someone in charge of the barbecue.
Evening call from the porch. Every 30 seconds you slap your forehead — the client thinks it’s your reaction to his ideas.
Accounting reminds you: the May holidays mean fewer working days, but the same targets.
A colleague is back from the May holidays, tanned and happy. You’re back with a report and a touch of envy.
right: Ask him to do your report

text: The Boss proposes “a short week with no lunch break — so we can leave early.” Lunch is sacred.
The first heat wave. The AC hasn’t been serviced yet and blows the smell of last summer.
HR wants the vacation schedule agreed by the end of the week. Everyone wants July. There’s only one July.
A colleague is going on vacation and leaving you “a couple of small things” — a four-page list.
The Boss asks why you leave at 6:00 when “it’s light out until eleven in summer.”
The intern had his graduation party, and this morning he shows up with a very mysterious face and his blazer inside out.
left: Cover for him with the Boss

text: The client writes: “Everyone’s on vacation, but the project must be delivered before July.” You’re not on vacation.
The department invites you to a summer terrace after work. You have an early call tomorrow.
Poplar fluff drifts in through the open window right into your keyboard. The Q key no longer works.
The Boss is going on vacation and leaving you “in charge.” No authority, all of the responsibility.
Three days until your vacation. Your inbox is overflowing, and your mind is already on the beach.
left: Clear it all before you go

text: HR announces “summer Fridays”: you can leave at 4:00 if everything’s done. Everything is never done.
93°F in the open space. A quiet war rages over the AC remote between “64°F” and “79°F.”
The office manager bought ice cream for everyone, but it’s one box for forty people.
The Boss has allowed shorts, but only “decent” ones. He didn’t define “decent.”
Three coworkers are on vacation, and their tasks are “temporarily” yours. Temporarily means until September.
right: Talk to the Boss about workload

text: A client from a hot country is surprised your office is hotter than his beach.
left: Move the meeting to a café

text: A thunderstorm, the lights are flickering, your laptop is at 5%, and the report isn’t saved.
Someone found an old fan in the storage room. It works, but it sounds like a jet taking off.
You’re on vacation. The Boss messages: “urgent, just for a minute.”
The department is going river rafting this weekend. You’ve never held a paddle.
Accounting wants your travel expenses for scorching July. Do receipts for iced coffee count?
It’s just you and the ficus in the office. So quiet you can hear it grow.
The Boss is back from vacation, tanned and full of ideas: “Let’s rebuild every process by September!”
Back to school is coming. Coworkers compare backpack prices and swap tutors’ numbers.
A colleague didn’t come back from vacation: “Stuck in the mountains, bad signal.” His tasks are now yours.
A colleague brought a sack of apples from his garden and is handing them out. Refusing is not an option.
HR announces fall planning: everyone gets a 10-page personal development plan.
A client suddenly revived after summer and wants everything “right now, before the season starts.”
Last week of summer, and you have unused vacation days. The Boss hints that “November would be better.”
Coworkers invite you out of town tonight to watch a meteor shower. Stand-up is at 9:00 tomorrow.
The ficus dried out while everyone was on vacation. The office manager is looking for someone to blame.
Everyone’s back from vacation. The Boss: “Rested? Great! Time to start living a new way.”
Forty minutes of beach photos in the meeting room. You’ve already seen three hundred sunsets.
September 1st: the traffic is back, and with it come late arrivals and school parent chats.
HR launches an “autumn reboot”: trainings every day at 8:30.
New interns have arrived. One was seated next to you “temporarily” — he asks a question a minute.
right: Hand him a manual and headphones

text: The first autumn downpour. Your umbrella is at home, and the subway is a 15-minute run.
left: Wait it out at the office

text: Accounting reminds you: two weeks until quarter end, and you have open invoices from July.
The coffee machine broke on the very first Monday of September. The office is in shock.
left: Do a coffee run for everyone

text: A colleague suggests signing up for a language class together. Classes are in the evenings.
The client is back from vacation and forgot what you agreed on in July. Back to square one.
Budget planning for next year begins. The Boss wants an “ambitious but realistic” plan.
Finance cuts the department budget by 20% and asks what you’re willing to give up.
Half the department is sneezing. You can feel you’re next.
HR offers flu shots right in the office. There’s a line by the meeting room and only one nurse.
Coworkers are preparing Halloween costumes and invite you to join a group look: “Deadline and Its Victims.”
You leave work — it’s already dark. When you arrived — it was dark too.
Accounting asks you to plan expenses for the year ahead, accurate to the cent.
For the budget defense, the Boss wants a presentation “Apple-style.” The only template you have is 2007-style.
A colleague suggests spending the rest of the budget before year end “just in case.” All of it at once.
The client is planning their budget too and asks if they can have “the same thing, but half the price.”
Seven weeks till year-end. The Boss: “Let’s finish everything we didn’t get to this year. Starting today.”
Accounting warns: all invoices by December 15. After that it’s “year-end close, nothing accepted”.
November. You last saw the sun in October. Same with motivation.
HR sends the annual review form: “Rate yourself on 18 competencies from 1 to 10”.
The department started planning the holiday party. Theme: “Hollywood”. You need a costume.
Black Friday: everyone is on sale sites. The office Wi‑Fi is barely breathing.
The client wants a six-month project done “before New Year”.
left: Take it on and make it
right: Split it into stages till spring

text: First snow. Half the office is photographing the window, the other half is stuck in traffic.
The Boss wants “the year in numbers” by Friday. The numbers aren’t great.
right: Show them as is, with a plan

text: A colleague already hung lights on their monitor. It’s November.
right: Ask them to take it down

text: The office manager asks for help decorating the tree. There’s one string of lights, and untangling it takes half a day.
Secret Santa: you drew a coworker you’ve never talked to.
At the holiday party the host calls you on stage for a balloon contest.
The Boss scans the room: “Someone has to be on call January 2nd.” His eyes stop on you.
Accounting is closing the year and wants all invoices by tonight. Half are in your inbox, half in your memory.
After the party, photos appear in the group chat. In one of them, you’re hugging the tree.
A box of tangerines arrived. An hour later there are only peels and holiday smell left.
HR wants a holiday video greeting from your department. The script is on you.
Dec 31, 4 PM. The client: “Don’t leave! One tiny 5-minute fix”.
right: Wish happy holidays and close the laptop

text: The department decides who plays Santa at the kids’ party. The costume is already on your chair.
